title: Lehigh Hanson Materials (Oct 2017 TCC) SR&ED Decision
subject: TCC Rule 58 preliminary motion on SR&ED eligibility for an alternative-fuels cement kiln project.
summary: Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 205, is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision in which Justice Lyons dismissed a Rule 58 motion over Lehigh's alternative-fuels cement kiln project. For Canadian taxpayers, the takeaway is that eligibility under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act turns on proven facts about experiments, not abstract legal questions.
metaDescription: Explore the October 2017 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision for Lehigh Hanson Materials and its impact on Canadian R&D claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
1.1 The Statutory and Administrative Framework for SR&ED in Canada

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program stands as the cornerstone of federal and provincial support for industrial innovation within Canada. Administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the program is codified under the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA"). The legislative mandate of the program is to incentivize Canadian businesses across all sectors to undertake systematic investigations that lead to technological advancements, thereby enhancing the global competitiveness of the Canadian economy. To access the highly beneficial Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) provided under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, and to fully deduct qualifying expenditures under section 37, taxpayers are required to demonstrate unequivocally that their activities satisfy the precise, heavily litigated legal definition of SR&ED set out in subsection 248(1) of the ITA.

Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED is legally defined as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statutory definition categorizes qualifying work into three distinct primary branches: basic research under paragraph (a), applied research under paragraph (b), and experimental development under paragraph (c). For the overwhelming majority of commercial and industrial enterprises operating in Canada, claims are filed under paragraph (c) as experimental development. This specific paragraph demands that the work be undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes. Furthermore, paragraph (d) provides for the inclusion of certain support activities—such as engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—provided these activities are commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the primary SR&ED work described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c).
1.2 The Taxpayer's Claim and the Procedural Posture

The dispute in Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 205, perfectly encapsulates the inherent tension between large-scale industrial manufacturing and the strict legal requirements of the SR&ED program. Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited (the "Applicant" or "Taxpayer"), a private Canadian corporation and wholly-owned subsidiary of a United Kingdom company, whose principal businesses were cement, ready-mixed concrete, aggregates and pipe and cement products, claimed SR&ED tax incentives for its taxation years ending December 31, 2009, December 31, 2010 and December 31, 2011 on the basis that its Delta Alternative Fuels Project (the "Project"), in which it used alternative fuels (including construction and demolition waste and mixed plastic and paper) in the cement kiln at its Delta, British Columbia plant, constituted eligible experimental development under paragraph (c) of subsection 248(1).

The Minister of National Revenue, following the CRA's SR&ED review of the claims, reassessed and denied the federal SR&ED credits, totaling $782,576, claimed by Lehigh for the relevant years, and also reduced the corresponding British Columbia SR&ED non-refundable tax credits. The Minister's disallowance was predicated on the position that it is common practice for cement kilns to use alternative fuels, so that there were no technological uncertainties and no technological advancements, and that any issues that arose while using alternative fuels could be resolved by applying known practices, techniques and methodologies; the activities were characterized as routine engineering and standard practice rather than a systematic investigation seeking to overcome a genuine technological uncertainty. After the CRA Appeals Division responded to the Taxpayer's notices of objection, the Taxpayer appealed to the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) (Docket 2015-2735(IT)G) to challenge the administrative disallowance and seek a judicial determination of eligibility.

During the pre-trial phases of this docket, the procedural complexity of the litigation was highlighted by the filing of a motion under Rule 58 of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure). A Rule 58 motion requests the determination of a question of law, fact, or mixed law and fact prior to the main hearing, often to expedite proceedings or narrow the scope of the dispute. Lehigh proposed the following question for determination: does "experimental development" as defined in paragraph (c) of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) constitute SR&ED even if other industry participants (located in or outside of Canada) have achieved the particular or a similar "technological advancement" in their particular circumstances? The Tax Court dismissed this preliminary motion, determining that the question was not properly raised in the pleadings, that it could not be answered conclusively in either direction, that it had no reasonable prospect of success, and that the disputed material facts, including the facts relating to Lehigh's experiments, required a full trial with viva voce, expert and documentary evidence. This procedural step underscores the highly factual, evidence-intensive nature of SR&ED litigation, where questions of law are inextricably bound to the granular technical realities of the taxpayer's operations.
1.3 The Court's Final Holding and Jurisprudential Standard

The Rule 58 motion was heard in Vancouver on November 24, 2016 before the Honourable Justice Kathleen Lyons, who issued her Reasons for Order on October 6, 2017. In her meticulously reasoned decision, Justice Lyons dismissed the Taxpayer's motion and awarded costs to the respondent in any event of the cause; the decision does not determine whether the experimental development work undertaken by Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited met the criteria mandated by the ITA, as that ultimate issue was left to the trial judge.

The legal foundation of the Court's analysis was the seminal jurisprudential test established by former Chief Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC). The Northwest Hydraulic framework, described by the Court as the leading authority for determining whether an activity constitutes SR&ED and applied extensively at the trial and appellate levels, articulates a five-question test (reproduced in Appendix I to the reasons), each question of which must be answered in the affirmative for work to qualify as SR&ED.

Justice Lyons measured Lehigh's proposed question against this five-factor test rather than evaluating the technical and documentary evidence on the merits. The Court concluded that the question was not determinative of any of the five factors, that whether other industry participants have achieved a particular or similar advancement is a relevant but not determinative fact for the first and fourth questions (technological uncertainty and technological advancement), and that the ultimate legal test depends on whether the identified uncertainty could be resolved by routine engineering or standard practices, being the techniques, procedures and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. Because the existence of technological uncertainty and the achievement of technological advancement formed the "factual crux" of the case, remained in dispute and could not be determined in a factual vacuum, the Court held that a trial with the evidentiary protections afforded to both sides was required before the activities could be classified as either eligible experimental development or standard practice.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The dismissal of the motion in Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited serves as a critical jurisprudential warning for large corporate taxpayers and their technical advisors. The judgment confirms that SR&ED eligibility cannot be settled through an abstract question of law and provides a clear map of the evidentiary and legal issues that a large-scale, capital-intensive industrial SR&ED claim must be prepared to prove at trial. The Tax Court of Canada operates strictly on the balance of probabilities, placing the initial onus of proof squarely upon the taxpayer to demolish the Minister's assumptions. The following subsections analyze the legal, technical, and documentation issues that the Minister's reassessment placed in dispute and that the Court identified as remaining for determination at trial.
2.1 The Conflation of Routine Engineering with Technological Uncertainty (Question 1)

The threshold requirement for any SR&ED claim under Canadian law, corresponding to the first question of the Northwest Hydraulic test, is the existence of a technological risk or uncertainty. As articulated by Justice Bowman and drawn upon by Justice Lyons in 2017 TCC 205, technological uncertainty exists only when the probability of achieving a given result or objective cannot be known or determined in advance on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience.

In the heavy materials manufacturing sector, companies routinely face severe operational challenges, including raw material variability, extreme thermal stress on equipment, and stringent environmental compliance standards. In the Lehigh Hanson proceeding, the question whether the issues and obstacles the Taxpayer encountered in using alternative fuels in its cement kiln constituted true technological uncertainties or merely difficult operational hurdles inherent to the business was placed squarely in dispute by the Minister's assumptions, but was not resolved by the Court, which held that it formed part of the factual crux of the case to be determined at trial.

The Court confirmed the line drawn in the jurisprudence between "routine engineering" and "technological uncertainty." Justice Bowman's clarification, adopted in this matter, states that technical risk or uncertainty must be such that it cannot be removed using standard procedures or by simply applying known engineering principles. The Court added that the fact that other industry participants have achieved a particular or similar advancement might well be indicative that there is no technological uncertainty, but that the ultimate determination depends on whether the identified uncertainty can be resolved by routine engineering or standard practices. To prove that standard engineering practices are insufficient, a taxpayer must therefore be prepared to comprehensively define what those standard practices are within its specific industrial context, and then demonstrate precisely why those practices fail to yield a solution.

The Minister's position was that the challenges faced by Lehigh Hanson, while undoubtedly difficult, highly time-consuming, and economically risky for the corporation, were resolvable through the application of known practices, techniques and methodologies, and that the use of alternative fuels in cement kilns was common practice. Lehigh denied that the technological advancements it sought were based on known practices, techniques and methodologies accessible to competent professionals in the field, and the Court did not decide the point. The ability to legally distinguish between a business or commercial uncertainty (e.g., "Can we optimize this kiln to run this new aggregate cost-effectively without halting production?") and a true technological uncertainty (e.g., "Do the fundamental laws of thermodynamics and material science permit these specific chemical compounds to bond under these precise thermal parameters without structural degradation?") will therefore be the central issue at trial, and the inability to draw that distinction remains a primary vector for the dismissal of any such claim.
2.2 The Absence of Formal Hypothesis Generation (Question 2)

The second prong of the Northwest Hydraulic criteria requires that the taxpayer formulate a hypothesis specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating the technological uncertainty identified in the first step. A hypothesis, in the context of the ITA, is an idea, rooted in existing scientific principles, that represents a proposed solution or anticipated outcome to the technological problem, which must then be subjected to empirical testing.

The decision in 2017 TCC 205 did not examine whether Lehigh's problem-solving mechanisms possessed the anticipatory rigor of hypothesis generation, because the evidence on the Project's methodology was not before the Court; Lehigh pleaded that it conducted "experimental trials" with alternative fuels at its Delta plant, while the Minister assumed that the work was routine engineering and standard practice. A claimant in Lehigh's position must nonetheless be prepared to prove this factor at trial. A critical methodological deficiency in many industrial claims is an ad-hoc, reactive approach to operational failures. When a production process yields substandard materials or encounters mechanical breakdown, the personnel involved often react by adjusting parameters on the fly, relying heavily on their vast institutional experience and intuition to stabilize the process.

Where a taxpayer engages in iterative testing, the courts distinguish between commercial troubleshooting (often termed "tinkering" in SR&ED jurisprudence) and eligible scientific experimentation. A legally valid hypothesis must be formulated a priori—before the physical testing begins. It must state the expected technical outcome and the scientific rationale behind that expectation. The failure to formalize and document hypotheses prior to modifying the production environment means that a court cannot view the subsequent work as a planned search for knowledge, but rather as standard industrial optimization.
2.3 Failure to Execute a Systematic Investigation (Question 3)

Subsection 248(1) explicitly and mandatorily requires a "systematic investigation or search". This statutory phrasing corresponds to the third question of the Northwest Hydraulic test, which asks whether the procedures adopted accord with established and objective principles of the scientific method.
A qualifying systematic investigation in the Canadian legal context requires a highly structured, logical progression:

items: Observation and Problem Definition: Identifying the precise limitation in the current state of technology.
Hypothesis Formulation: Documenting a proposed, testable solution based on theoretical reasoning.
Testing and Experimentation: Controlled execution of the hypothesis where variables are strictly isolated and monitored.
Analysis and Conclusion: Evaluating the empirical data against the initial hypothesis and feeding the results back into a new iterative cycle if necessary.

body.text: In Lehigh Hanson, the Court did not make findings on whether the procedures adopted by the Taxpayer accorded with these objective principles; it held instead that facts relating to experiments are critical to a SR&ED analysis and that, without such facts, the eligibility question could not be answered, which is why the matter had to proceed to a full hearing. A common weakness in such claims is an insufficient separation between standard commercial production runs and experimental trial runs. In a continuous heavy manufacturing environment, failing to isolate variables is catastrophic to an SR&ED claim. If plant engineers adjust kiln temperature, airflow, and feed rate simultaneously in an attempt to restore production quality, it becomes scientifically impossible to determine which variable caused a subsequent success or failure. Without controlled variables, it is impossible for the Court to ascertain whether a successful outcome was the result of a genuine technological breakthrough or merely a fortuitous combination of standard operational adjustments. Justice Lyons' insistence that the facts of the experiments be proven at trial means that, absent a controlled Design of Experiments (DOE) framework, such work risks being indistinguishable from routine plant maintenance and quality control.
2.4 The Insufficiency of Contemporaneous Documentation (Question 5)

Perhaps the most pervasive and potentially fatal evidentiary risk identified in the Northwest Hydraulic test, reproduced by Justice Lyons in Appendix I to her reasons in Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen, is the lack of adequate contemporaneous documentation. Within the Tax Court of Canada, oral testimony provided years after the fact by engineers, plant managers, or corporate executives is viewed with intense judicial scrutiny and skepticism. Human memory is inherently fallible, and the financial temptation for ex post facto rationalization—recasting routine operational issues as profound technological uncertainties strictly to secure lucrative tax credits—is recognized by the courts as a significant risk.

The Court requires contemporaneous documentation—records generated at the exact time the work was occurring, not summarized months or years later by tax consultants for the express purpose of surviving a CRA audit. In Lehigh Hanson, the Court made no finding about the Taxpayer's documentation; it did, however, note that the disputed material facts underpinning the proposed question would require viva voce evidence, including expert evidence, and documentary evidence, confirming that the Taxpayer's records would be central at trial.
Proper contemporaneous documentation expected by the TCC, particularly for entities of Lehigh Hanson's sophistication, includes:

items: Formal project charter documents detailing the baseline technology and the specific technological leap attempted.
Laboratory notebooks, digitally time-stamped or physically signed and dated by technical staff.
Detailed iteration logs showing exactly what variables were changed in each test, the raw data results, and the analytical conclusions drawn from that specific iteration.
Internal email correspondence between engineering teams actively debating the theoretical physics, chemistry, or engineering principles underlying a failure.
Test protocols, matrices, and formal failure analysis logs.

body.text: A failure to maintain this level of granular, timeline-based evidence would severely undermine a taxpayer's credibility. The decision makes clear that, without contemporaneous records strictly tracking the execution of the "systematic investigation" and the evolution of the "technological advancement," a taxpayer in Lehigh's position would struggle to meet its strict burden of proof at trial. A lack of documentation would essentially force the Court to view the entirety of the activities through the lens of ordinary, commercially motivated engineering work.
2.5 Failure to Prove the Generation of Technological Advancement (Question 4)

The final substantive legal issue, flowing naturally from the procedural issues above, is the requirement to prove that the work sought or achieved a technological advancement. Paragraph (c) of the definition of SR&ED requires that the work be undertaken for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes.

It is a fundamental tenet of Canadian tax jurisprudence that technological advancement is not measured by the commercial success of the product, nor is it measured by achieving a novel feature that simply combines known technologies in a new way. It is measured exclusively by the generation of new technological knowledge that advances the general understanding within the company or the broader industry. Crucially, even a completely failed project can result in a technological advancement if it systematically proves that a certain hypothesis is invalid, thereby adding to the internal repository of scientific knowledge and preventing future dead-ends.

In 2017 TCC 205, Justice Lyons addressed this factor only in the context of Lehigh's proposed question. Lehigh had admitted that cement industry participants, in and outside of Canada, had undertaken work and achieved advancements with respect to the use of alternative fuels in cement kilns that were the same as or similar to those sought in the Project, but it denied that the Project did not advance the general understanding of cement industry participants and other knowledgeable persons in the field. Drawing on Justice Bowman's analysis of the fourth question, the Court agreed that a technological advance made by a taxpayer does not cease to be one merely because other industry participants may have achieved the particular or similar advancement, unless that other participant's work in achieving that advancement is known or available to persons knowledgeable in the field. Overcoming a problem using standard practices does not generate new technological knowledge; it merely demonstrates the competent, albeit arduous, application of existing knowledge. Whether the Project merely brought the company up to standard industry operational norms or generated an eligible technological advancement under the purpose test of paragraph (c) was accordingly left to be determined on the evidence at trial.
3. Comparative Summary Table

To synthesize the complex intersection of statutory requirements, administrative policy, and judicial interpretation, the following table maps the legal requirements for SR&ED eligibility against the status of each issue in the Lehigh Hanson case, alongside the strict standard of proof imposed by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Status of the Issue in 2017 TCC 205 (Minister's Assumptions, Taxpayer's Pleadings and the Court's Observations)
TCC Standard of Proof & Required Contemporaneous Evidence

cells: Q1: Technological Uncertainty Was there a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be resolved by routine engineering or standard practice?

The Minister assumed that using alternative fuels in cement kilns is common practice and that there were no technological uncertainties at the Delta plant; the Taxpayer pleaded that it carried out a systematic investigation of the technical uncertainties related to the use of alternative fuels. The Court held that the achievements of other industry participants may be indicative of the absence of uncertainty but are not determinative; the issue was left for trial.

Burden of Proof: High. Evidence Required: Documented technological baseline. Proof that standard practices (handbooks, existing IP, routine calculation) were objectively insufficient to achieve the goal, demonstrating a gap in applied science.
Q2: Formulation of a Hypothesis Did the taxpayer formulate a hypothesis specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating the uncertainty?

Not examined in the decision. The Court noted that every question in the five-factor test must be answered in the affirmative for work to qualify as SR&ED, and that facts relating to experiments are critical, leaving the Taxpayer to prove its hypotheses at trial.

Burden of Proof: Strict. Evidence Required: Written hypotheses predating the actual experimental work. Clear theoretical and technical justification for why the proposed experimental solution might succeed where standard practice fails.
Q3: Systematic Investigation Did the procedure adopted accord with established and objective principles of the scientific method?

Not examined in the decision. The Taxpayer pleaded that it conducted "experimental trials" with alternative fuels, the Minister pleaded that the activities were routine engineering and standard practice, and the Court held that the resulting factual dispute required viva voce, expert and documentary evidence at a full trial.

Burden of Proof: High. Evidence Required: Test matrices, Design of Experiments (DOE) protocols, controlled trial documentation, and clear separation of R&D execution phases from commercial manufacturing and quality control phases.
Q4: Technological Advancement Did the process result in a technological advancement (the generation of new technological knowledge)?

The Taxpayer admitted that other industry participants had achieved the same or similar advancements, but denied that the advancements it sought were based on known practices accessible to competent professionals and denied that the Project failed to advance general understanding; the Minister denied that any advancement was sought or achieved. The Court held that an advance does not cease to be one merely because others may have achieved it, unless their work was known or available to knowledgeable persons.

Burden of Proof: Moderate to High. Evidence Required: Documentation of the specific new knowledge generated. Internal technical memos detailing "lessons learned" regarding the underlying physics, chemistry, or core engineering principles, regardless of commercial success.
Q5: Contemporaneous Documentation Was a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests and results kept as the work progressed?
Not examined in the decision. The Court reproduced the requirement in Appendix I to its reasons and noted that documentary evidence would be needed to resolve the disputed material facts at trial.

Burden of Proof: Extremely Strict. Evidence Required: Time-stamped laboratory notebooks, continuous iteration logs, signed technical meeting minutes, daily engineering reports, SCADA data dumps aligned with test runs, and integrated time-tracking software linked to R&D codes.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To fully comprehend the sweeping legal and technical implications of Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen (2017 TCC 205), theoretical legal analysis must be rigorously bridged with practical industrial application. The Tax Court of Canada does not exist in a vacuum; its rulings directly dictate how engineers and corporate tax directors must govern their daily operations.

The following two applied case studies construct realistic, highly detailed industrial scenarios facing the exact legal and methodological pitfalls placed in issue by the Minister's reassessment in Lehigh Hanson and left by Justice Lyons for determination at trial. For each scenario, a comprehensive, step-by-step remediation plan is provided. These plans demonstrate precisely how a sophisticated Canadian taxpayer must restructure project governance, technical documentation, inter-departmental workflows, and experimentation tracking to satisfy the rigorous demands of subsection 248(1) of the ITA and survive the Northwest Hydraulic scrutiny.
4.1 Case Study A: Heavy Materials Manufacturer Developing Low-Carbon Cementitious Alternatives
4.1.1 The Scenario and Identifying the Legal Pitfalls

A large Canadian heavy materials manufacturer, "Boreal Aggregates Inc.," is attempting to develop a novel, highly sustainable, low-carbon supplementary cementitious material (SCM). Their goal is to replace 40% of the traditional Portland cement clinker with a proprietary blend of uncalcined local clay and raw volcanic ash, drastically reducing the thermal energy required in the kiln and lowering overall CO2 emissions. This mirrors the heavy industrial, continuous-manufacturing context of Lehigh Hanson.

The Initial Approach (The Pitfall): Driven by commercial pressure to release a "green" product, Boreal Aggregates' plant managers bypass formal R&D protocols. They simply begin adding varying ratios of the clay and ash mixture into the massive rotary kiln during standard commercial production runs. When the resulting concrete batches fail standard ASTM compressive strength tests (becoming far too brittle), the operators reactively adjust the kiln temperature, alter the draft fan speeds, and tweak the admixture ratios simultaneously based on their intuition and decades of plant experience.

They maintain only high-level production logs indicating: "Batch 44: Failed - Too brittle," and "Batch 45: Adjusted temp up 50 degrees, slowed feed - Passed." At the end of the fiscal year, the corporate finance department identifies this massive expenditure of time, energy, and ruined raw materials. They retroactively interview the plant managers, compile a spreadsheet of wasted costs, and draft a generalized SR&ED T661 claim stating, "We faced massive technological uncertainty in making low-carbon cement and overcame it through extensive, costly testing."

If subjected to a CRA technical review or audited and appealed to the TCC, this claim will undoubtedly face the same position that the Minister took against the taxpayer in Lehigh Hanson (2017 TCC 205). The Minister's experts will classify this exclusively as routine engineering (trial-and-error by experienced professionals) resolvable by known practices, techniques and methodologies, note the complete absence of the scientific method (no isolated variables), and reject the claim entirely due to a fatal lack of contemporaneous documentation; and, as Lehigh Hanson confirms, the taxpayer will not be able to escape that factual dispute through a preliminary question of law but will have to prove the facts of its experiments at a full trial.
4.1.2 Remediation Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Operational Directives

Before any physical raw materials are mixed, Boreal Aggregates must formally and structurally charter the SR&ED project. The technical governance must be forcibly integrated with financial oversight to prevent ad-hoc production tinkering.

items: Establishment of a Technical Steering Committee: The project must be governed by qualified materials scientists and chemical engineers, not solely by plant production managers whose primary mandate is throughput and yield.

Implementation of Internal R&D Contracts (Work Orders): Standard operating procedures across the entire corporation must be amended to mandate an approved "R&D Work Order" before commercial production equipment can be diverted for experimental trials. This internal document must explicitly define the time frame, the budget allocation, and specifically articulate the technological uncertainty justifying the diversion of commercial assets.

Financial Segregation and Contractor Rules: If external metallurgical laboratories are utilized for raw material scanning (e.g., X-ray diffraction), the commercial contracts must explicitly state that the sub-contractor is performing experimental development on behalf of Boreal Aggregates. This ensures compliance with the strict Canadian rules on third-party SR&ED payments and guarantees the retention of intellectual property rights, a prerequisite for claiming the expenditures.

body.text: 4.1.3 Remediation Step 2: Defining Technological Uncertainty and Establishing Hypotheses

To pass Question 1 and Question 2 of the Northwest Hydraulic test, Boreal Aggregates cannot simply rely on the commercial unknown ("we didn't know if the cement would sell or be strong enough"). They must isolate the exact scientific variables causing the uncertainty.

items: Documenting the Baseline of Technology: Boreal must produce a formal "State of Technology Report" (a 3-5 page internal technical memo) prior to the work. This memo must cite current industry literature and explicitly state: "Standard practice dictates that introducing uncalcined clay directly into the milling process reduces the reactive calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H) matrix formation by 30%, resulting in brittle failure. Routine engineering cannot predict how the specific, unmapped amorphous mineralogy of our local volcanic ash will interact with the uncalcined clay under 1200°C kiln conditions to offset this severe degradation."

Formulating the Verifiable Hypothesis: Prior to initiating Batch 44, the lead chemical engineer must document a highly specific, testable hypothesis: "Hypothesis: By introducing a proprietary high-shear mechanical mixing phase prior to thermal calcination, we hypothesize that the amorphous silica in the volcanic ash will act as a rapid nucleating agent, forcing the uncalcined clay to integrate completely into the C-S-H matrix without requiring standard peak calcination temperatures, thereby preserving baseline compressive strength while lowering thermal load."

body.text: 4.1.4 Remediation Step 3: Executing and Tracking the Systematic Investigation
To satisfy Question 3 (systematic investigation), the reactive trial-and-error approach must be entirely replaced with a rigorous Design of Experiments (DOE).

items: Strict Control of Variables: The engineering team must establish a testing matrix where only a single variable (e.g., kiln temperature, shear mixing time, or specific ash-to-clay mass ratio) is altered per test batch.

Systemic Separation of R&D from Production: During these experimental batches, the plant is officially designated as operating in "R&D Mode." This status must be electronically reflected in the plant's SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) system logs, cleanly separating commercial production downtime from eligible experimental runtime.

Rigorous Data Analysis: When a test batch fails, the reason for failure must be scientifically analyzed via advanced means (e.g., scanning electron microscopy to view the failed C-S-H bonds), rather than relying on a plant operator's visual inspection of brittleness. The resulting empirical data must be used to refine the hypothesis for the next controlled iteration.

body.text: 4.1.5 Remediation Step 4: Technical Documentation Alignment with CRA Standards

To avoid the contemporaneous documentation risk inherent in the fifth factor of the Northwest Hydraulic test, reproduced by Justice Lyons in Appendix I to her reasons, Boreal Aggregates must implement an unassailable documentation strategy tailored to survive CRA scrutiny.

items: The Centralized R&D Ledger: Establish a centralized, tamper-evident digital repository (e.g., a secured SharePoint site or specialized R&D tracking software) that automatically time-stamps all entries, rendering ex post facto fabrication impossible.

Mandatory Weekly SR&ED Logs: Technical leads must mandate a strict Friday afternoon logging session detailing: (1) Experimental work executed this week, (2) Specific variables tested against the hypothesis, (3) Empirical data outcomes, and (4) Formulated next steps.

Granular Time Tracking: All employees involved—from the lead chemical engineer down to the floor operator monitoring the specific R&D batch—must track their time continuously. The timesheets must feature specific codes mapping directly to the approved R&D Work Orders, completely eliminating the use of a generic, highly suspect "R&D" time bucket.

body.text: By instituting this rigid, scientifically sound structure, Boreal Aggregates ensures that if audited or challenged in the Tax Court of Canada, they possess a continuous, time-stamped evidentiary trail that conclusively proves technological uncertainty, systematic investigation, and the generation of technological advancement, directly nullifying the objections raised by the Minister in Lehigh Hanson.
4.2 Case Study B: Infrastructure Engineering Firm Designing Novel Hydrodemolition Containment Systems
4.2.1 The Scenario and Identifying the Legal Pitfalls

"Apex Hydro-Tech Ltd." is a sophisticated infrastructure engineering and services firm specializing in advanced hydrodemolition (utilizing ultra-high-pressure water jets exceeding 20,000 PSI to remove deteriorated concrete from critical infrastructure like bridge decks). They secure a highly lucrative contract to rehabilitate a major bridge spanning a highly sensitive ecological waterway. Standard industry containment systems leak under high pressure, causing severe environmental violations. To win the bid, Apex commits to designing a completely novel, automated, negative-pressure containment shroud that attaches directly to their robotic hydro-milling tractors to capture 100% of the slurry.

The Initial Approach (The Pitfall): The mechanical design team utilizes standard CAD software to design a new, larger shroud. They fabricate a prototype in the metal shop, bolt it to the tractor, and immediately deploy it to the bridge site. It fails catastrophically on the first day, leaking slurry into the river. The on-site mechanics and welders react immediately: they weld additional steel baffling into the shroud and install a massively upsized vacuum pump over the next two weeks until the leaking finally ceases. At year-end, Apex files a T661 claiming the entire design, fabrication, and frantic on-site adjustment process as SR&ED.

The CRA denies the claim in its entirety. The RTA cites that the work was simply routine engineering design and standard "field-fitting"—a direct parallel to the Minister's position in Lehigh Hanson that the taxpayer's activities constituted routine engineering and standard practice. The CRA argues that any competent mechanical engineer could have solved a leak by adding baffles and a bigger pump. Apex failed to prove that a systemic uncertainty existed beyond basic mechanical integration and scale-up.
4.2.2 Remediation Step 1: Restructuring the R&D Charter (Moving Beyond Routine Design)

Apex must fundamentally understand that standard mechanical design—even if the final product is novel, highly customized, or eventually patented—is not automatically SR&ED under the ITA. The Tax Court strictly distinguishes between routine engineering design (applying known physics and geometries to a new shape) and experimental development (facing a genuine gap in the underlying technological knowledge).

items: Defining the Fundamental Knowledge Gap: Before claiming the project, Apex's Chief Engineer must isolate the exact technological uncertainty. The core issue isn't simply "making a box that doesn't leak." The issue must be rooted deeply in the physics of fluid dynamics and multiphase flow.

Establishing the Baseline Documentation: Apex must comprehensively document that standard computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling cannot accurately simulate the highly chaotic, multiphase flow (composed of liquid water, solid concrete slurry, and high-velocity displaced air) generated within a confined mechanical shroud operating at 20,000 PSI against a highly irregular, degrading concrete surface. Apex must prove, in writing, that standard engineering calculations and existing modeling software are fundamentally insufficient to determine the optimal internal geometry required for total negative pressure maintenance.

body.text: 4.2.3 Remediation Step 2: Formulating Verifiable Hypotheses in Fluid Dynamics
To escape the CRA's classification of mere "field-fitting" or "tinkering," Apex must establish a robust scientific hypothesis before the mechanics strike an arc on the bridge site.

items: The Pre-Fabrication Hypothesis: "Hypothesis: By engineering a dual-chamber shroud incorporating an internal cyclonic separation geometry angled precisely at 15 degrees relative to the primary water jet, we hypothesize that we can induce an artificial, sustained vortex that will keep the heavier concrete slurry in suspension long enough for a standard 500 CFM vacuum to evacuate the primary chamber without causing cavitation or localized pressure blowouts at the irregular mechanical seal interface."
This specific hypothesis elevates the work from "let's build a box and see if it leaks" to a highly targeted, eligible investigation of applied fluid dynamics and pressure vessel engineering.

body.text: 4.2.4 Remediation Step 3: Executing Systematic Investigation vs. On-Site Troubleshooting

The Tax Court of Canada and the CRA strictly scrutinize any work performed on commercial job sites (like an active bridge repair). The CRA routinely views on-site work as commercial execution rather than experimentation. Apex must aggressively ring-fence the experimental phase.

items: Proving Systematic Iteration: When the first prototype fails on the bridge, the subsequent welding and pump adjustments absolutely cannot be random or reactionary. Apex must establish a formal field-testing protocol.

Advanced Data Capture: During the field test, Apex must install pressure transducers and flow meters inside the shroud to measure the real-time vacuum fluctuations and slurry velocity. When the leak occurs, they must capture the raw telemetry data showing exactly why the vortex failed (e.g., documenting that internal pressure dropped below the critical threshold at the rear seal).

Iterative, Science-Based Design: The site mechanics do not just weld a random baffle to stop the leak. The engineering team analyzes the pressure transducer data, alters the CFD model based on the real-world telemetry, and formally designs a specific geometric baffle modification calculated to intentionally alter the fluid flow. This modification is then fabricated and tested in the next highly controlled iteration.

body.text: 4.2.5 Remediation Step 4: Structuring Contemporaneous Documentation for Field R&D

Field-based SR&ED claims fail with extraordinary frequency because documentation is routinely left to site foremen who track progress strictly in commercial terms ("Bridge deck 50% cleared today") rather than scientific terms.

items: Mandatory Field Test Reports (FTR): Apex must mandate the use of standardized, highly technical FTR forms deployed on the ruggedized tablets of site supervisors. Every single time the robotic tractor is halted for a shroud modification, an FTR must be generated detailing the variables altered.

Photographic and Telemetry Evidence Alignment: The TCC responds highly favorably to visual and data-driven contemporaneous evidence that corroborates written logs. Apex should maintain a secure server where daily, date-stamped photos of the internal shroud modifications are uploaded and explicitly cross-referenced with the pressure transducer data logs captured during that exact day's test run.

Strict Separation of Commercial vs. Eligible Costs: Apex must clearly, financially document which operating hours were spent actually hydro-milling the concrete to advance the commercial contract (commercial work, mostly ineligible) versus the hours spent running the tractor solely to test the fluid dynamics and seal integrity of the new shroud design (eligible experimental development).

body.text: By proactively establishing a technological baseline, formulating hypotheses rooted strictly in fluid dynamics, utilizing sensor-driven systematic testing, and maintaining rigorous, time-stamped field documentation, Apex Hydro-Tech Ltd. effectively neutralizes the legal vulnerabilities placed in issue in Lehigh Hanson and standardizes a highly defensible, structurally sound SR&ED operating procedure.
5. Conclusion and Strategic Policy Outlook

The Tax Court of Canada's ruling in Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen (2017 TCC 205) serves as a definitive judicial reaffirmation that the stringent boundaries governing the Scientific Research and Experimental Development program are applied to the facts of a taxpayer's own experiments, under the Northwest Hydraulic five-question test, and cannot be settled through an abstract question of law determined before trial. Justice Lyons' refusal to answer Lehigh's proposed question in a factual vacuum, and her confirmation that the ultimate test is whether an identified uncertainty could be resolved by routine engineering or standard practice, underscore a persistent and vital reality within Canadian tax jurisprudence: the statutory definition of experimental development encoded in paragraph (c) of subsection 248(1) is neither a financial subsidy for complex commercial troubleshooting nor a retroactive reward for routine, albeit incredibly difficult and costly, industrial engineering.

For large industrial, manufacturing, and engineering taxpayers operating within Canada's borders, the primary directive emerging from this jurisprudence is the absolute, non-negotiable necessity of proactive, technologically precise, and contemporaneously documented project governance. The courts have repeatedly demonstrated an exceedingly low tolerance for ex post facto rationalizations—the practice of allowing financial departments to retroactively mold standard production challenges into scientific hypotheses simply to harvest tax credits. Taxpayers must recognize that the legal burden of proof rests entirely and heavily upon them to establish the baseline of standard technological practice, to scientifically isolate the technological risk, and to systematically document the generation of new technological knowledge.

Ultimately, mastering the SR&ED legislative framework requires a profound operational paradigm shift within the corporate structure. It necessitates aggressively breaking down the traditional communication silos that exist between the plant floor, the engineering design department, and the corporate tax function. By legally integrating strict scientific method protocols and rigorous contemporaneous documentation requirements directly into standard operating and production procedures, Canadian businesses can effectively transform the glaring legal vulnerabilities highlighted in Lehigh Hanson into robust, highly defensible frameworks for maximizing their legitimate entitlements under the ITA's premier innovation incentive program.

outcome: Motion dismissed; court held SR&ED eligibility depends on proven trial facts and cannot be decided on a Rule 58 motion.
